title: The Shape of Home
subtitle: Stars Between the Strings · Chapter 12 of 40
content:
The shape of home changed when I started leaving things in two places.

At first, it was accidental. A spare shirt ended up in Greg's van after a sudden rainstorm. Then my toothbrush appeared in the small bathroom cabinet because Greg had bought one and said it looked lonely in the package.

“You can take it back,” he said when I noticed it.

“It’s a toothbrush.”

“A toothbrush with choices.”

“You are projecting.”

“I do that with household objects.”

The toothbrush stayed.

My scarf remained on the moon-shaped hook. My tea found a permanent place beside Greg's coffee. A stack of my books leaned against the record shelf, and one of my mugs occupied the corner of his kitchenette as though it had always belonged there.

I told myself not to read too much into it.

Then Mara offered me work at the community center.

The job was part-time, mostly organizing supplies, answering questions, and helping coordinate the evening music sessions. It was not a grand career. It paid enough to keep the bakery from swallowing my entire budget. More importantly, it gave my days a shape that belonged to me.

When I told Greg, he lifted me off the ground.

“Put me down,” I said, laughing.

“I’m celebrating.”

“You’re celebrating with my spine.”

He set I down immediately. “Sorry.”

“You may celebrate with a kiss.”

“That sounds like a reward.”

“It is a mutually beneficial arrangement.”

He kissed me in the middle of the community center hallway while Mara watched from behind a stack of folding chairs.

“Get a room,” she called.

Greg pulled back. “We have several.”

“That was not an invitation to discuss them.”

I buried my face in Greg's shoulder.

The weeks that followed were gentle in the way a new routine could be gentle. I worked mornings at the center. Greg played afternoon sets at the car wash or helped Steven with errands. Evenings belonged to shared meals, bad television, and music that spilled through the apartment until the neighbors threatened to complain.

I learned the small geography of his life. Which drawer held the good utensils. Which record made him dance while cooking. How he became quiet when he was worried about Steven. How he sang nonsense lyrics when he could not find the right words.

Greg learned mine. He learned when I needed company and when company meant sitting in another room. He learned which jokes helped and which ones cut too close. He learned that I hated being surprised by touch from behind, and he never forgot.

The first time he remembered without being reminded, I cried in the grocery store.

Greg stood beside the cart, holding a package of tea. “Did I do something?”

“No.”

“That’s usually not the answer people give while crying near the cereal.”

I wiped my face. “You remembered.”

He understood. “Oh.”

“You remembered.”

“Of course I did.”

The words were not dismissive. They were baffled. As if remembering the shape of my comfort was the easiest thing in the world.

I leaned against him. He placed one hand on my shoulder, giving me time to move away.

“I’m going to buy the tea,” I whispered.

“I support this.”

“Then I’m going to buy the expensive cereal.”

“I support this less.”

“You can make up the difference with music.”

“I accept.”

When I returned to the apartment, Greg had rearranged the living room. The record shelf stood against the wall. The old chair was gone. In its place was a small couch with enough room for two people and a lamp that cast warm light instead of making the ceiling look haunted.

I stopped in the doorway.

“What is this?”

“A couch.”

“I can see that.”

“I was told I needed to be more precise.”

I walked into the room. The couch was deep and soft. One end held a folded blanket. The other held a pillow in the color I liked.

“You bought a couch.”

“It was on sale.”

“Greg.”

“Mara said the old chair was becoming a safety concern.”

“So you bought a couch.”

“A chair is just a couch with fewer opportunities.”

I touched the armrest. “How much did it cost?”

“Less than the emotional value of the record shelf.”

“That is not an answer.”

“I used money I saved from a gig.”

My throat tightened. “You didn’t have to do that.”

“I wanted a place where you could sit without judging the furniture.”

“I’m still going to judge it.”

“I know.”

I turned toward him. “Are you trying to make me move in?”

The question changed the air.

Greg's smile faded. “No.”

“You have my toothbrush. My books. My scarf. Now a couch.”

“I bought a couch because I wanted a couch.”

“For us?”

“For the room.”

“That’s not what I asked.”

Greg stepped closer, then stopped. “I want a life with you. I don’t want to lure you into one with furniture.”

My chest hurt.

“I’m not saying no,” I said.

“I know.”

“I’m saying I need to know that this is a choice.”

“It is.”

“For both of us.”

“Yes.”

The room was quiet except for the refrigerator. Greg looked nervous now, not charming, not amused. The sincerity made him seem younger and older at once.

“I don’t want to replace your life,” he said. “I don’t want to be the reason you stop having your own place, your own work, your own friends. I want to be the person you come home to because you have chosen me, not because you have nowhere else to go.”

I had no defense against that.

“I want to choose you,” I said.

He swallowed. “Then we’ll keep making choices.”

I crossed the space between us. “Can I sit on the couch?”

“Please.”

I sat. The cushions gave beneath me. Greg sat beside me, close enough that my thighs touched.

“It’s nice,” I said.

“I’m relieved.”

“It could use a blanket.”

He pulled the folded one over both my laps.

“Better.”

“I am a man of solutions.”

“You’re a man of blankets.”

“That’s more accurate.”

I leaned into him. Greg wrapped one arm around my shoulders. His mouth brushed my hair.

“Do you want to stay tonight?” he asked.

“I live upstairs.”

“I know.”

“Do you want me to?”

“Yes.”

“Then yes.”

He kissed me slowly. The couch held us both. The lamp glowed. The new room did not feel like a trap.

It felt like space being made.

Later, when I woke from a nap with Greg's arm around me, my phone rested on the table beside his. Two lives, still separate, touching at the edges.

I had not moved in.

But I had stayed.

That evening, I returned to my own studio and opened every cabinet. The room looked different because I did. The mug on the counter was mine. The scarf in the van was mine. The photograph on Greg's shelf was mine. None of those things required me to surrender the rest of myself.

I called Greg while I folded laundry.

“Are you calling to complain about the couch?” he asked.

“I’m calling to inform you that it has survived another day.”

“A brave piece of furniture.”

“It has also acquired a blanket.”

“Did you leave it there?”

“Maybe.”

He laughed. “You’re doing it again.”

“I’m allowed to have range.”

The next box Greg brought upstairs contained a lamp, a packet of old guitar strings and a photograph of him with Steven when Steven was small.

“Uh, I might've overpacked,” he said.

“You brought three things.”

“Emotionally, that's a whole moving truck.”

He balanced the frame against the windowsill. He hadn't hung it because he wasn't sure whether I wanted it in my apartment. I looked at the boy in the picture, the way Greg stood half bent to match his height, and the awkward little smile caught between them.

“Steven should still have a place in your life when you're here,” I said.

“Yeah. I know. It's just sometimes I worry I'll make this place into the van with better plumbing.”

“I like the van.”

“Don't tell the van. It'll never stop bragging.”

I moved my books aside and made room for the photograph on the shelf. Greg didn't interpret that as an invitation to move everything he owned into my room.

“I want to ask you something,” I said. “When I say I prefer polyamory, that doesn't mean every person I love has access to every place I live. It means the people involved get to negotiate it.”

He nodded. “Right. Like how I don't show up at Steven's place just because I'm his dad. Except, y'know, more dating and less embarrassing childhood photos.”

“Exactly.”

“So this shelf is your shelf. My picture can visit. My junk drawer does not get automatic citizenship.”

“Your junk drawer needs a passport.”

“Forget a passport. It needs a hazmat team.”

He laughed, but he asked before he left the lamp. I said yes to the lamp and no to the strings. They went back into his bag, and he didn't treat it as rejection.


I folded a shirt and placed it in the drawer. “I’m scared of how easy it is to be with you.”

Greg's voice softened. “Why?”

“Because easy things have never stayed easy.”

“Then we’ll pay attention when they change.”

“You make it sound like maintenance.”

“Love is maintenance. Also music and pastries and occasional dramatic staring.”

“You’re very committed to the pastries.”

“They have never abandoned me.”

“You have been abandoned by a pastry.”

“Once. It was a danish.”

I smiled and sat on the edge of my bed.

“Do you want to come over?” he asked.

“I thought you wanted me to choose.”

“I’m asking, not deciding.”

I looked around my own room. “I’ll come after I finish this.”

“I’ll leave the door open.”

“You have a lock now.”

“I can leave it unlocked.”

“That is not the same thing.”

“I know.”

I finished folding the laundry. Then I walked downstairs, crossed the street, and entered Greg's apartment with my own key.

The couch was waiting. So was he.

The ease between us was not proof that nothing would change.

It was proof that I had learned how to speak when it did.

I stayed until midnight, then walked back upstairs with my own key in my hand and Greg's laughter following me through the stairwell. The studio was still small. The bakery still woke I before dawn. Nothing about the lease had changed.

But I placed the photograph on my own shelf beside the empty space where the tea belonged, and the room answered with a quiet sense of recognition.

Home, I was learning, did not have to be a single address. It could be a pattern of places where my body stopped preparing to leave.
